rationale: Gold requires CAPEC-66 (SQL Injection) plus its four execution steps (capec:attack-pattern:66:step:1..4). The narrative paraphrases all four steps in the correct order and with content that maps directly onto the evidence: "surveying the application's functionality" = step:1 ("[Survey application] ... inventory of the functionality exposed"); "determines which user-controllable inputs are susceptible to injection by testing special SQL characters" = step:2 ("Determine the user-controllable input susceptible to injection... attempt to inject characters that have special meaning in SQL"); "experimenting with the vulnerabilities to hypothesize the underlying query and iteratively adding logic to extract or modify information" = step:3 ("hypothesize what the underlying query looks like. Iteratively try to add logic ... extract information ... or modify or delete information"); "exploits the vulnerability by crafting and executing the refined SQL query to reveal, modify, or delete database data" = step:4 ("craft and execute the underlying SQL query ... reveal, modify, and/or delete database data"). No invented facts — every clause traces to the corresponding ExecutionStep description in logic_flow.results[0].records[0].related. The only weakness is provenance mechanics: the structured "claims" array cites only CAPEC-66 (primary_id) and never lists the four capec:attack-pattern:66:step:N ids as explicit entity_ids/citations, so an automated id-matcher over claims alone would show 0/4 step coverage even though the prose itself fully and correctly surfaces all four steps in order. That gap costs groundedness but not correctness/faithfulness/completeness of the actual answer delivered to the analyst.
